About this document

This document provides the teaching content for Digital Technologies Year 11 of the
New Zealand Curriculum. Equivalent for Te Marautanga o Aotearoa is being
published separately.

Progress and assessment information for Digital Technologies Year 11 is still in
development. Once that is completed, Digital Technologies Year 11 is proposed to
be made by the Minister of Education as a National Curriculum Statement under
section 90(1)(a) of the Education and Training Act 2020.

It is proposed that, once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, schools
who offer Digital Technologies Year 11 will be required to start using it in Year 11
from 1 January 2028.

This document will be replaced with the official version made under the Act and
published in the New Zealand Gazette once that has occurred.

  In Digital Technologies, students develop knowledge and skills through either              Digital Technologies provide pathways into senior Technology and related
  Digital Technologies or Electronics and Mechatronics. In Digital Technologies              courses in Years 12 and 13.
  students explore computational thinking and programming, digital media
  foundations and project development, and artificial intelligence and emerging
  technologies. In Electronics and Mechatronics, students explore sensing and
  measurement, actuation and response, control of system behaviour, and system
  integration. Across both strands, students design, develop, test, refine, and
  evaluate technological outcomes in response to authentic needs, opportunities,
  users, and contexts.

Through the study of Digital Technologies, students are taught how to investigate
needs and opportunities, design purposeful outcomes, and develop, test, refine, and
evaluate their work. Depending on the strand selected, students apply knowledge and
practices from computational thinking and programming, digital media, or electronics
and mechatronic systems to create outcomes for specific users, purposes, and
contexts.

Digital Technologies provides students with the knowledge and practices to combine
creative design, technical development, and technological problem-solving. Students
learn to communicate and refine ideas, select and apply appropriate tools,
techniques, and processes, and use evidence from testing and feedback to improve
outcomes. They develop their understanding of how digital and technological systems
work and how design and technical decisions influence functionality, reliability,
usability, and the experiences of users and communities.

As students progress through Year 11 Digital Technologies, they develop greater
independence in making and explaining design and technical decisions. They
consider factors such as purpose, functionality, usability, accessibility, reliability,
sustainability, privacy, cultural considerations, and responsible practice, and use
research, feedback, testing, and evaluation to improve the quality and fitness for
purpose of their outcomes

                            Development and evaluation
                             Digital media development involves creating, sourcing, adapting, organising,
                              editing, and integrating the assets, content, and technical components needed to
                              produce a coherent and functional outcome. What is created depends on the
                              selected digital media context.
                              o Interactive experiences may require interfaces or screens, interaction states,
                                navigation, rules or logic, feedback, levels or scenes, data, and digital assets.
                              o Information experiences may require pages or screens, content and data
                                structures, navigation, search or filtering functions, data visualisations, and
                                digital assets.
                              o Time-based experiences may require shots, scenes or sequences, animation
                                or video, audio, timing and pacing, transitions, titles or captions, and suitable
                                output formats.
                             Technical quality is demonstrated through the purposeful creation and integration
                              of components, reliable functionality, appropriate file and output quality,
                              consistency, accessibility, and suitability for the intended platform and use.
                             Testing checks whether components and the developing outcome work as
                              intended. Depending on the selected context, testing may focus on functionality,
                              usability, readability, accessibility, layout, interaction, timing, pacing, playback,
                              file quality, platform suitability, conventions, technical quality, or responsible
                              practice.
                             Feedback from users, audiences or community can provide information about
                              whether the outcome is clear, usable, engaging, appropriate, fit-for-purpose, and
                              enhances the mana of the people using it.
                             A final digital media outcome works as intended when it meets the project
                              purpose, suits the users, audience, or community, follows relevant conventions,
                              applies responsible practice, and functions appropriately for the selected context
                              and platform.
                             Evaluation uses evidence from the project purpose, requirements, testing,
                              feedback, and the final outcome to judge how well the outcome meets its
                              purpose and the needs of the users, audience, or community.
